primer.mng_p_world.title: The people of the felt walls
primer.mng_p_world.text: You were born among the Mongols - the nomads of the great steppe between the Altai and the Khingan. There are no cities or ploughland here: wealth means horses, sheep, camels and the people who follow your standard. Whoever the clans will follow rules, and great matters are settled by the kurultai, an assembly of the nobles. Over everything stands the Eternal Blue Sky, which, the Mongols believe, grants power to the one it has chosen.
primer.mng_p_world_clans.title: The steppe before Chinggis
primer.mng_p_world_clans.text: You were born at a time when the steppe still knows no single khan. Mongols, Tatars, Kereits, Naimans and Merkits each roam for themselves, steal one another's herds and wives and avenge blood with blood. The Chinese Jin empire to the south plays them off against each other. "The starry sky was turning," the chronicle will later say, "the whole earth was in turmoil; no one slept in his own bed."
primer.mng_p_world_chinggis.title: Chinggis Khan
primer.mng_p_world_chinggis.text: You were born in the years of Chinggis Khan. In 1206 a kurultai on the Onon proclaimed Temüjin khan of all "the peoples who live behind felt walls". He broke up the clans into tens, hundreds and thousands under his own nökers and founded the keshig guard, the relay post and the law - the yasa. Now the steppe is one, and its tümens are riding against China and west, towards Khwarazm.
primer.mng_p_world_empire.title: The Great Empire
primer.mng_p_world_empire.text: You were born in a great age: the sons and grandsons of Chinggis rule an empire from Korea to Hungary. The Great Khan sits at Karakorum, and his kinsmen hold the uluses: the Jochids on the Volga, the Chagatayids in Central Asia. Couriers gallop from yam to yam, and merchants travel the caravan roads under the protection of the khan's paiza. It seems that the whole world will become Mongol.
primer.mng_p_world_uluses.title: The four uluses
primer.mng_p_world_uluses.text: You were born when the empire had broken into four realms. Khubilai's Yuan rules China and the steppe, the Golden Horde the Volga and Rus, the Ilkhans Iran, the Chagatayids Central Asia. The khans still think of themselves as one family, yet they war with one another and live more and more by the customs of the conquered: in China in the Chinese way, in Iran and on the Volga in the Muslim way.
primer.mng_p_world_north.title: The Northern Yuan
primer.mng_p_world_north.text: You were born after the Mongols had been driven out of China. The khans have returned to the steppe, but their power is weak: the eastern Mongols and the western Oirats cut each other down for supremacy, and the Ming to the south build walls and close the markets. Without Chinese grain, tea and iron life is hard, and raids on the border are the only way to force China to trade.
primer.mng_p_society.title: White bone and black bone
primer.mng_p_society.text: At the top is the "white bone": the Golden Lineage of the Chinggisids and the noyans, the leaders of thousands. Beneath them are the nökers - sworn warrior-retainers. The backbone of the people are the arats, the "black bone", ordinary herders. Lower still are the bo'ol, hereditary servants of another clan, and captive slaves. But on the steppe everything is shifting: a loyal nöker can become a commander of a thousand, and a noyan who loses at the kurultai a herdsman.
primer.mng_p_society_yuan.title: The four classes
primer.mng_p_society_yuan.text: In the Yuan empire subjects are divided into four classes. First come the Mongols. Second the semu, "people of various kinds": Uyghurs, Muslims, Tanguts, even Europeans - they serve as officials and tax-gatherers. Third the Hanren, the northern Chinese. Last the Nanren, people of the former Southern Song. Your class decides your posts, your punishments and even your right to bear arms.
primer.mng_p_society_slave.title: The bo'ol
primer.mng_p_society_slave.text: You were born into a family of bo'ol - hereditary servants. Your forebears may have been taken in a raid, or may have put themselves under a strong clan of their own will. A bo'ol herds another's livestock, pitches another's yurts and follows his master to war. Yet even a bo'ol can rise: for a brave deed or loyalty his lord may declare him a darkhan - free of all dues.
primer.mng_p_birth.title: Born in a yurt
primer.mng_p_birth.text: You were born in a yurt, on a felt by the hearth. The midwife cut the cord, and over the door a sign was hung - an arrow for a boy, a red ribbon for a girl - so that visitors would know and not come in. After three days the mother gets up with the baby, and the family brings gifts: a lamb, a foal, a length of cloth. The name is often taken from the first thing seen, or is a "bad" name to fool the evil spirits.
primer.mng_p_childhood.title: In the saddle at three
primer.mng_p_childhood.text: Mongol children are put on a horse at three and tied to the saddle; by five they are riding on their own. Boys and girls herd lambs, gather argal, milk goats and shoot little bows at sacks of wool. In winter they play shagai with sheep's anklebones. Here children learn not from books but by doing: by twelve a child can do almost everything the steppe demands.
primer.mng_p_childhood_city.title: Children of the capital
primer.mng_p_childhood_city.text: In the city the children of the nobility are taught differently: schools at court teach the Uyghur, Chinese or Persian script, reckoning and the laws. Yet even here the boys are taken to the riding ground every day to shoot from the saddle: a Mongol who has forgotten how to ride is no longer a Mongol.
primer.mng_p_home.title: The yurt
primer.mng_p_home.text: Your home is a yurt, a ger: lattice walls (khana), roof poles (uni), the toono ring at the top and two or three layers of felt. It goes up in an hour and travels on two camels. The door faces south, the hearth is in the middle, the men's side with the harness is on the left, the women's side with the vessels on the right, and opposite the door is the place of honour with the ongons. The threshold is "the neck of the house": stepping on it is a bad omen.
primer.mng_p_home_move.title: Four camps
primer.mng_p_home_move.text: In a year a family moves camp four or five times: the winter camp in a hollow sheltered from the wind, the spring camp where the snow melts first and the lambs are born, the summer camp by a river with tall grass, the autumn camp where the herds fatten before winter. Pastures are shared out among the clans, and a stranger's grazing can be paid for in blood.
primer.mng_p_food.title: White food and red food
primer.mng_p_food.text: In summer the Mongols live on "white food": kumis of mare's milk, aaruul curds, cream skins, cheese. In winter on "red food": boiled mutton, borts dried meat, horseflesh. They eat almost no vegetables, and bread and millet are bartered from settled neighbours. Kumis is drunk by the pailful, and at feasts arkhi milk spirit too. The first drop is always flicked to the Sky.
primer.mng_p_clothes.title: The deel
primer.mng_p_clothes.text: Men and women wear the deel - a long robe wrapped over to the right and belted with a broad sash, in which they carry a knife, a flint and a bowl. In winter it is lined with sheepskin, in summer it is of silk or cotton. On their feet are boots with upturned toes, so as not to wound the earth. Noblewomen wear the tall boqta headdress decorated with feathers - it can be seen above a crowd from far off.
primer.mng_p_faith.title: The Eternal Blue Sky
primer.mng_p_faith.text: The Mongols believe in Tengri, the Eternal Blue Sky, and in Etügen, Mother Earth. Spirits dwell everywhere: in mountains, rivers and the hearth. The ancestors are kept in ongons, little felt figures above the place of honour. On the passes ovoo cairns hung with ribbons are built. Shamans and udagan women speak with the spirits to the drum. Thunder is feared most of all: whoever is struck by lightning bears the anger of the Sky.
primer.mng_p_faith_many.title: Every faith under one Sky
primer.mng_p_faith_many.text: The khans tolerate every faith so long as it prays for the khan: at court Nestorian priests, Buddhist monks, Muslim mullahs and Daoists argue with one another. Many of the khatuns are Christians of the Kereit clan, and the merchants are Muslims. Clergy of every faith are freed from taxes, and a Mongol may light a candle in church in the morning and flick kumis to the Sky in the evening.
primer.mng_p_faith_islam.title: Islam on the Volga
primer.mng_p_faith_islam.text: Ever since Khan Özbeg proclaimed Islam the faith of the Horde, mosques and madrasas have been going up in Sarai and the nobles have been learning Arabic prayers. But the steppe folk still live largely in the old way: they drink kumis, honour the ancestors, and Chinggis's yasa means no less to them than the Quran. The Russian church stands in Sarai too - its bishop holds a patent from the khan.
primer.mng_p_faith_buddhist.title: The Yellow Faith
primer.mng_p_faith_buddhist.text: The lamas in yellow hats teach that all living things are reborn, and that suffering ends only for one who follows the Buddha's path. Khan Khubilai made the Tibetan lama Phagpa preceptor of the empire, and after 1578 Buddhism reached the most distant camps: altars with little burkhan figures are set up in the yurts, juniper is burned and prayer wheels are turned.
primer.mng_p_work.title: The herd is everything
primer.mng_p_work.text: A Mongol counts wealth not in money but in head of livestock. Horses are for war and honour, sheep for food and felt, camels and oxen for moving camp, goats for down. The men herd and break the horses; the women milk, churn kumis, make felt and sew. Craftsmen are mostly captives, and trade is in the hands of Uyghur and Muslim ortaq merchants. The worst disaster is the dzud, a winter of ice when the herds starve.
primer.mng_p_work_city.title: A city of craftsmen
primer.mng_p_work_city.text: The city lives off the khan's court: thousands of captive craftsmen - Chinese weavers, Persian jewellers, Russian carpenters - work for the treasury. Ortaq merchants take silver from the nobles and carry it with the caravans as partners. Taxes are levied by census, and the trade tax - the tamgha - is taken on every deal.
primer.mng_p_place_onon.title: The Onon and Kherlen
primer.mng_p_place_onon.text: Your land is the upper Onon and Kherlen by the sacred mountain Burkhan Khaldun, where, by tradition, Chinggis was born. Hills grown with larch, broad valleys of feather grass, rivers that freeze to the bottom in winter. Summers are hot, winters bring forty degrees of frost. These are the pastures of the Borjigin - Chinggis's clan - and here the Mongols came back after every campaign.
primer.mng_p_place_karakorum.title: Karakorum
primer.mng_p_place_karakorum.text: Karakorum stands in the Orkhon valley, where the Turkic khagans and the Uyghurs once had their seats. The city is small - the friar Rubruck compared it to a suburb of Paris - but here the roads of the whole empire meet: envoys from Rome and Korea, merchants from Baghdad and Samarkand, captive craftsmen from all over the world. Round the walls stand yurts and herds.
primer.mng_p_place_khanbaliq.title: Khanbaliq
primer.mng_p_place_khanbaliq.text: Khanbaliq, the "khan's city", Dadu in Chinese, was built by Khubilai to a plan: a square of walls with eleven gates, straight streets, palaces on lakes. A canal links it to the granaries of the south, and in the markets people pay with paper money. The Mongol nobles live in palaces, but in the palace park stand yurts, and grass brought from the steppe grows there.
primer.mng_p_place_sarai.title: Sarai
primer.mng_p_place_sarai.text: Sarai stands on the Akhtuba, an arm of the Volga. It is a city without walls - who would dare attack the khan's seat? There are quarters of Mongols, Kipchaks, Circassians, Russians and Greeks; mosques, bathhouses, potters' workshops with turquoise glaze. In winter the Horde stands by the Volga, and in spring it moves out to the steppe and the city empties.
primer.mng_p_place_tabriz.title: Tabriz
primer.mng_p_place_tabriz.text: Tabriz is the trading capital of the Ilkhans on the road from China to Europe: Genoese and Venetians, Armenians and Jews, merchants from India come here. The Mongols live not in the city but in tents on the nearby pastures - Ujan and Mughan - and ride into town as its masters. Persian viziers run the government, Mongol noyans the army.
primer.mng_p_place.title: The great steppe
primer.mng_p_place.text: The steppe runs from Manchuria to Hungary - thousands of versts of grass across which you can ride for months. In the south the Gobi desert separates it from China, in the north the taiga. Water is scarce, trees scarcer still, and the wind hardly ever drops. But to a nomad it is the richest land in the world: grass gives livestock, and livestock gives everything else.
primer.mng_p_law.title: The yasa
primer.mng_p_law.text: The law of the steppe is the yasa, the ordinances of Chinggis. Death for murder, horse theft, treason, lying before a judge, flight from battle, harbouring a runaway slave. One must not urinate into water, bathe in a river in summer or step on the threshold of the khan's yurt. Soldiers are judged by their ten: all answer for the fault of one. Judgement is given by a darughachi or a noyan, and the empire's chief judge was Chinggis's own adopted brother, Shigi Khutukhu.
primer.mng_p_health.title: Shaman and physician
primer.mng_p_health.text: Illness, in steppe belief, is an evil spirit that has entered a person. The shaman drives it out with the drum and an offering, and healers treat with kumis, mutton broth, cautery and bloodletting. At the khan's court Chinese and Persian doctors serve: they feel the pulse and set needles. A cord with a rag is hung over a sick person's yurt - strangers must not enter. Small children die most often, and grown men on campaign and in falls from horses.
primer.mng_p_women.title: The khatun
primer.mng_p_women.text: Mongol women are freer than those of their settled neighbours: they ride, shoot with the bow, trade and run the household, and while their husbands are on campaign they govern the camps. Chinggis's mother Hö'elün raised her children alone, Tolui's widow Sorghaghtani put her sons on the throne, and Mandukhai led armies. A bride is taken from another clan for a bride-price, and a widow often marries her husband's brother.
primer.mng_p_leisure.title: The three manly games
primer.mng_p_leisure.text: The great festival of summer is the naadam with its "three manly games": wrestling, horse racing and archery. The jockeys are children, the wrestlers dance the "eagle's flight", and women may shoot too. In winter people celebrate the White Month, the new year: they go round the yurts and bow to their elders. In the evenings they listen to storytellers with the khuur and play shagai and riddles, while the nobles stage ring hunts spanning hundreds of versts.
primer.mng_p_knowledge.title: Writing from top to bottom
primer.mng_p_knowledge.text: The Mongols had no writing of their own until 1204, when Chinggis had a captive Uyghur teach his sons. The Uyghur script is written from top to bottom; under Khubilai the lama Phagpa also created a "square" script for all the languages of the empire. The Secret History was written down around 1240. Bichechi scribes are trained at the courts, while ordinary herders know their genealogies nine generations back and hundreds of songs by heart.
primer.mng_p_war.title: The tümens
primer.mng_p_war.text: Every man from fifteen to sixty is a soldier. The army is divided into tens, hundreds, thousands and tümens of ten thousand. Each warrior has three to five horses, a bow that shoots three hundred paces, a sabre, a lasso and dried meat. The tümens ride a hundred versts a day, feign retreat and encircle the enemy, and take cities with the siege engines of captive craftsmen. To flee from battle means death for the whole ten.
primer.mng_p_war_yoke.title: The Horde's tribute
primer.mng_p_war_yoke.text: The Russian principalities pay the Horde its "exit" - tribute in silver and furs - and the princes travel to Sarai for a patent to rule. At first the tribute was gathered by baskaks; later the princes collected it themselves - and the princes of Moscow rose to power that way. The Horde punishes the disobedient with raids, but its own troubles more and more often give Rus a breathing space.
